did.abstract: This collection includes oral histories, photographic materials, and research materials collected for and created by the West Indian Carnival Documentation Project, undertaken by the Brooklyn History Society and the Brooklyn Museum in the mid-1990s. The project attempted to supplement existing scholarship on New York's West Indian American community and the West Indian American Day Carnival with oral histories and collected materials from community members and Carnival participants.

bioghist.head: Historical Note
bioghist.p: The Brooklyn Historical Society launched The West Indian Carnival (WIADC) Documentation Project in 1993 in cooperation with the West Indian American Day Carnival Association (WIADCA) and the Brooklyn Museum to supplement existing histories of Brooklyn Carnival with personal narratives, life histories of Carnival participants, and photographs of Carnival preparation. The WIADC Documentation Project attempted to capture different viewpoints within the hierarchy of Carnival organization and participation, with the broader goal of documenting the development and social and cultural functions of Brooklyn's West Indian population.

Two Co-Directors led the WIADC Documentation Project: Bill Pincheon, then a Ph.D. candidate in the Folklore Institute at Indiana University, and Dwandalyn (Dwan) Recce King, then the Chief Curator of the Brooklyn Historical Society. Additional project staff included interviewer Michael Roberts, research assistant Joyce Quamina, project assistant Megan McShea, and project fieldworkers Maureen Mahon and Kristen Elmquist, along with a scholarly advisory board that consulted with staff. Photographers Paul Lewis and Hayden Celestin were hired to assist with shooting the more behind-the-scenes aspects of the West Indian American Day Carnival—such as mas camps, mas makers and designers, band leaders, and steel pan orchestras—instead of the Carnival itself, for which a large amount of professional and amateur photographic documentation already existed.

WIADC Documentation Project staff conducted thirty-four interviews with individuals involved with the Carnival at all levels, including WIADCA President Carlos Lezama and other WIADCA staff, masquerade band leaders and costume designers, steel pan orchestra members, and Carnival participants and vendors. These interviews documented personal and cultural connections to Brooklyn Carnival and Carnival celebrations in countries of origin, as well as the administration and labor involved in organizing the event, forming mas bands and creating costumes, and performing in the parade.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: This collection contains oral histories, photographic material, and compiled research materials relating to the West Indian American Day Carnival (WIADC). The materials were collected and created as part of the documentation project undertaken by the Brooklyn Historical Society and the Brooklyn Museum.

Project staff conducted thirty-three oral history interviews, originally recorded on portable cassette tapes, to document the experiences of those involved with the WIADC, including Carnival organizers and staff members of the West Indian American Day Carnival Association (WIADCA), mas band leaders and designers, and Carnival participants and performers. These oral histories contain descriptions of life in the West Indies and Caribbean and immigration from countries in these regions; descriptions of Carnival celebrations in West Indian and Caribbean countries; the development of the WIADC and the WIADCA; mas bands and mas camps; traditional music, such as calypso, soca, and steel orchestras; and clashes between Carnival participants and residents in Brooklyn, specifically Jewish residents and members of Chabad Lubavitch.

This collection includes 477 prints, 179 negative film strips, and 18 photographic contact sheets. Subjects include mas bands and mas camps, steel pan orchestras, the Carnival and Kiddies Carnival, community events, and portraits of band leaders, band designers, and community figures.

Research materials gathered for the documentation project include clippings and publications; WIADCA flyers and programs; distribution and promotional materials from mas bands; and ephemera from Caribbean and West Indian events and exhibitions.

odd.head: Oral History Note
odd.p: Oral history interviews are intimate conversations between two people, both of whom have generously agreed to share these recordings with the Center for Brooklyn History archives and with researchers. Please listen in the spirit with which these were shared. Researchers will understand that:

1. The Center for Brooklyn History abides by the General Principles & Best Practices for Oral History as agreed upon by the Oral History Association (2009) and expects that use of this material will be done with respect for these professional ethics.

2. Every oral history relies on the memories, views, and opinions of the narrator. Because of the personal nature of oral history, listeners may find some viewpoints or language of the recorded participants to be objectionable. In keeping with its mission of preservation and unfettered access whenever possible, CBH presents these views as recorded.

3. Transcripts created prior to 2008 serve as a guide to the interview and are not considered verbatim. The audio recording should be considered the primary source for each interview. It may contain natural false starts, verbal stumbles, misspeaks, repetitions that are common in conversation, and other passages and phrases omitted from the transcript. This decision was made because CBH gives primacy to the audible voice and also because some researchers do find useful information in these verbal patterns.

4. Unless these verbal patterns are germane to your scholarly work, when quoting from this material, researchers are encouraged to correct the grammar and make other modifications, maintaining the flavor of the narrator's speech while editing the material for the standards of print.

dao.xlink:title: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Val Adams

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Val Adams

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Valentine "Val" Adams was born in St. Patrick parish in Grenada in 1956. Raised in a musical family, he began performing at an early age and achieved success in his teens while playing in the local Calypso band, Gary and the Rhythmeers. A decorated football player in Grenada, Adams first came to New York in 1974 after being selected to tour the city with the Grenada national football team. Soon after this visit, he immigrated to Brooklyn at eighteen years old to attend Hunter College and later Nassau Community College, where he studied accounting and music. Adams continued playing Calypso music in New York and eventually formed his own group, Val Adams and Exodus, which became a fixture at Grenadian functions in New York City.
Adams was instrumental in increasing Grenadian participation and introducing Shortknee, a traditional masquerade in Grenada, to the West Indian American Day Carnival.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: In the interview, Val Adams discusses his musical beginnings and his participation in Carnival in Grenada with particular reference to local mas genres, Jab Jab and Shortknee. He discusses his early impressions of Brooklyn and talks at some length about his continued musical career in New York. He discusses his involvement with the Carnival on Eastern Parkway and his attempts to increase Grenadian participation despite some resistance. Adams describes his impressions of the Brooklyn Carnival as a unique expression of pan-Caribbean unity and African American culture. Adams compares regional differences in Carnival traditions, how the Brooklyn Carnival has changed over time, the economic benefits, and some of the challenges facing the celebration. Interview conducted by Michael Roberts.

dao.xlink:title: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Jeffrey Adolphus

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Jeffrey Adolphus

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Jeffrey Adolphus was born in Belize circa 1952. He immigrated to Brooklyn in 1971 after completing high school. After moving to Brooklyn, he became a full-time musician, playing keyboard in his band, The Web. After The Web disbanded, Adolphus completed a five-year music program at The Muse, worked for United Airlines, Wells Fargo, the Young Men's Christian Association (YMCA), and the Board of Education, where he worked at the time of this interview.

Adolphus was instrumental in getting New York's Belizeans officially involved in the West Indian American Day Carnival parade in 1991 through his organization, the Belizean Carnival and Recreational Association (BECRA).

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: In the interview, Jeffrey Adolphus discusses his initial impressions of Brooklyn and his early efforts to gain Belizean entry into the West Indian Carnival parade. He contrasts Belizean, New Yorker, and Trinidadian attitudes toward the parade and describes the role of New York and Miami Belizeans in reinvigorating the Carnival tradition in Belize. Adolphus describes his personal connection to the parade with detailed discussions of selecting themes and designing costumes. He describes Belizean culture's mélange of ethnic traditions and emphasizes the parade's importance in promoting and disseminating Belizean culture and identity. Adolphus discusses fundraising, the challenges involved in organizing a parade contingent, and changes he'd like to see, including the importance of reaching out to the general African American community. Interview conducted by Dwan Reece King.

dao.xlink:title: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Jean Alexander

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Jean Alexander

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Jean Alexander was born and raised in St. Joseph, Trinidad, and is of East Indian descent. Married at fifteen, she traveled with her husband and children twice to the United States in 1963 and 1968 before permanently immigrating in 1971. The family moved to Brooklyn in 1975.

Alexander worked for the West Indian American Day Carnival Association (WIADCA) for forty-one years as the Director of Marketing and Public Relations before retiring in 2018. She is now the Co-Founder and Executive Director of the Caribbean American Center.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: In the interview, Jean Alexander discusses the role that class played in how one participated in Carnival in Trinidad. Introduced to the West Indian American Day Carnival Association (WIADCA) in 1974, she soon became involved as its public relations director, a position she still held in 1994, at the time of the interview. She reflects on the Carnival experience and considers the economic resources the Carnival brings to New York City each year. She notes that the Caribbean community's contributions have not been fully acknowledged by the government or the media. Alexander suggests that WIADCA should be a year-round institution that serves the community by providing resources for job training and employment and addressing the organization's need to involve more people from other Caribbean islands. She also discusses the cultural conflicts that have occurred among organizers and finishes with a description of the activities and services provided by the non-profit Caribbean American Center, of which WIADCA was an affiliate. Interview conducted by Dwan Reece King.

dao.xlink:title: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Randy Brewster

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Randy Brewster

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Randolph "Randy" Brewster was born in Trinidad and came to New York in 1961. He began participating in Carnival as a young boy in Trinidad and continued after immigrating to New York, where he is a band leader in the West Indian American Day Carnival.

Along with his partner Francis "Jackie" Clavery, Brewster founded the Culture of Black Creation, a costume design and production shop serving New York, Westchester, and Trinidad. Brewster was also a longtime member of the West Indian American Day Carnival Association, where he introduced community outreach initiatives and costume design education programs. At the time of the 1994 interview, he worked as a dental technician. Brewster passed away in 2023.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: In the interview, Randy Brewster recalls his early involvement with Carnival in Trinidad. He discusses developing carnival themes and the intrigue involved in keeping them secret with some elaboration on the judging criteria in Trinidad versus Brooklyn. He then describes the sketching and design process with his production partner, Jackie Clavery, and they discuss the hierarchy of carnival competition. Brewster discusses what Carnival means to him and regrets the lack of costume preservation. He describes the scope and logistics of the production process and discusses both positive and negative aspects of the Brooklyn parade, including the difference between a parade and a carnival or street festival (gumbi). He notes the emphasis on novelty each year and the pleasure he gets from watching youth involvement in the Kiddies Carnival, including that of his own children. Interview conducted by Dwan Reece King.

dao.xlink:title: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Winston Brewster

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Winston Brewster

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Winston Brewster was born in San Fernando, Trinidad. In 1969, at the age of thirty, he immigrated to the United States. Brewster first lived in Queens, where his family was located. He then moved to Brooklyn, where he still resided at the time of this interview, in 1995. While he participated in mas in Trinidad, he did not participate in Brooklyn. Instead, Brewster was involved as a vendor of Trinidadian food. When not preparing to sell food at his two stalls, he worked as a welder.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: In this interview, Winston Brewster discusses his involvement as a food vendor at Brooklyn's West Indian Carnival. He reflects on the Carnival's early days in the late 1960s, noting changes in the route, the number of spectators, and how food vending has evolved. He also notes parallels between the Brooklyn Carnival and the Trinidadian Carnival. Brewster discusses the Carnival's impact on the Caribbean community and the wider New York community, noting growing multicultural participation. He considers the Carnival's enormity and suggests that the cultural presence can and has influenced the city's political decisions. Interview conducted by Dwan Reece King.

dao.xlink:title: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Cheryl Byron

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Cheryl Byron

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Cheryl Byron was born in Trinidad and was an active social and cultural advocate, dancer, poet, and painter from a young age. Byron immigrated to New York in 1974 and received her bachelor's and master's degrees in English from City College, City University of New York. At the time of the 1994 interview, Byron was teaching at Medgar Evers College, Fort Greene Senior Citizens Center, and John Houseman Berean Church. She was also pursuing a PhD in Performance and Museum Studies at New York University and writing her dissertation about the Brooklyn Carnival.

Byron was a pioneer of Rapso and Dub Poetry, and was the first poet to perform these genres in a calypso tent at Carnival in Trinidad. She studied dance with Pearl Primus and later joined the Primus Border Earth Theater. In 1981, Byron founded Something Positive, Inc., a New York City-based performing arts and education organization working to preserve the art and culture of the African diaspora. Cheryl Byron died of cancer in 2003.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: In the interview, Cheryl Byron recalls her early participation playing mas in Carnival in Trinidad and, since the 1970s, as a dancer and poet in the Brooklyn parade. She describes developing ideas and concepts for her old mas band and what Carnival represents to her personally. Much of the interview focuses on the intricacy and ritualism involved in parade preparations and the history of the satirical genre of old mas/J'ouvert. She describes some of the positive and negative aspects of the parade, including the greater ethnic inclusion and the growing participation of children, the poor organization, random violence, and the decreased presence of live music. She suggests means of improvement. Noting common misconceptions surrounding Carnival, Byron suggests community education as a possible solution. She ends by noting the potential to garner greater government support and calls for a tighter network among the diasporic Caribbean Carnivals. Interview conducted by Michael Roberts.

dao.xlink:title: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Glenda Cadogan

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Glenda Cadogan

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Glenda Cadogan was born in Trinidad, where she studied at the University of the West Indies and worked as a civil servant, then as a journalist. Cadogan immigrated to New York in 1988, studied journalism at New York University, and continued as a journalist with the City Sun. In addition to the Sun, Cadogan wrote for Caribbean Life, New York Amsterdam News, and the Immigrant's Journal.

Along with Nandi Keyi, Cadogan cofounded the Sapodilla Sisters, a production company that produces plays and performances showcasing Caribbean culture. Cadogan also founded Mauby Media Services, a media consultancy firm.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: In the interview, Glenda Cadogan recalls her first impressions of Brooklyn. She describes herself as a "calypso junkie" and recalls covering the Carnival in Trinidad as a journalist. Cadogan notes differences between the Brooklyn and Trinidad Carnivals, including organization and levels of participation. She describes her personal connection to Carnival and notes the positive messages the parade sends and its potential as a political catalyst. Cadogan suggests ways to raise awareness of the parade outside the community, distinguishes between the concepts of "parade" and "Carnival," and calls for more mainstream marketing and advertising outside the community. She describes the recent tensions between the Hasidim and Caribbean communities and her modest hopes for bridge-building. She notes recent changes in Brooklyn's Carnival and the connection between local economics and Carnival participation. She is hopeful about the Kiddies Carnival. Cadogan lists her favorite aspects of Carnival and what she sees as its negative aspects. Cadogan closes by recognizing the achievements of the West Indian American Day Carnival Association (WIADCA) and calling for innovation within its ranks through an infusion of younger blood. Interview conducted by Michael Roberts.

dao.xlink:title: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Kelvin "Fuzzy" Davis

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Kelvin "Fuzzy" Davis

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Francis "Jackie" Clavery was born in Trinidad in 1928 and worked building refineries in Saint Croix. Clavery immigrated to New York in 1966 and moved to Brooklyn in 1977.
He designed and created costumes with Randy Brewster as part of The Culture of Black Creation. He was one of only four designers in Trinidad who worked with copper in Carnival designs.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: In the interview, Clavery recalls getting involved in designing costumes for the Brooklyn parade with Randy Brewster. He describes the research process involved in realizing a band's theme. He discusses deficiencies in New York's judging process and the higher standard of competition in Trinidad. Clavery describes and demonstrates copper engraving, a rare technique he incorporates into his costumes. He explains the need to stay in touch with Trinidad's Carnival in order to keep an edge and stay innovative. Clavery then discusses his personal connection to Carnival. He traces the history of Carnival and describes Trinidad as a unique Caribbean multi-racial melting pot exhibiting more racial harmony than the United States. Interview conducted by Dwan Reece King.

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Kelvin "Fuzzy" Davis was born in Port of Spain, Trinidad, in 1945. He immigrated to Connecticut in 1968, then to Brooklyn in 1980, where he worked as a director overseeing emergency repairs for the City of New York.

Davis is an influential costume designer and builder for Brooklyn's Carnival and helped found the large mas bands Borokeet and Midas International. At the 2008 Carnival, he participated with the band Pieces of a Dream. In 2010, he was recorded as a panelist and interviewed as an artist for the Black Brooklyn Renaissance Digital Archive.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: In the interview, Davis describes the theme of his band Borokeet and assesses the Carnival in Brooklyn. He describes the serious negative effects of policing and the conflict with the Hasidim on the most recent parade of 1994. Davis appeals to the Caribbean community to coalesce and seize political power, especially given the economic benefits the Carnival brings to Brooklyn. He recounts his history with Carnival and his personal connections and training with high-profile designers and organizers. He describes modern designers' collaborative efforts and how a mas band brings its theme to life. He describes his commitment to and love for Carnival, along with some of the logistics and costs involved. Davis describes changes in Carnival and the commercialization of Trinidad's Carnival. He appeals for greater future collaboration between bands and the West Indian American Day Carnival Association. Davis compares Brooklyn's Carnival with others and regrets its lack of recognition. He ends with a call for national acceptance of the Brooklyn Carnival. Interview conducted by Dwan Reece King.

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Paula Davis was born in Trinidad and came to New York in 1969 to join family members. She headed her first mas band, the U.S.S. Maple, in 1980. Soon after, she founded Aquarium Productions and worked closely with her boyfriend, Clyde Bascombe, the band's designer. As Aquarium's bandleader, Davis was one of the few women bandleaders in the community. As of 2016, Aquarium has won at many carnivals over the previous thirty-five years, including both Children and Adult Band of the Year categories. They have received over 140 trophies and certificates from carnivals in New York, New Jersey, Baltimore, Philadelphia, and Orlando.

Davis begins with a brief description of her origins, immigration, and formative Carnival experiences. She closes with a critique of the process and bias among the judges who award prizes in the band competitions. Interview conducted by Dwan Reece King.

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Angela Dublin

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Angela Dublin was born in Curaçao. As a child, her family immigrated to Trinidad and Tobago. In Trinidad, she participated in the Carnival for two years as a child. In 1967, Dublin immigrated to the United States and settled in Brooklyn, New York, where she participates in the Brooklyn West Indian American Day Carnival.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: In this interview, Angela Dublin describes her immigration to the United States. She reflects on the West Indian community's interaction in the seventies. Dublin describes her childhood Carnival experiences in Trinidad, comparing the event's historical premise with her personal experience. She also provides detailed histories of the Carnival traditions of Dimanche Gras, calypso, and pan music. Dublin discusses the 1994 Carnival, noting the participation of international bands and media. She expresses frustration that although the Carnival generates revenue for the city, it still receives little local media coverage. There is also a discussion of a conflict with the Hasidic Jewish community and their desire to reschedule the Carnival because of the Jewish New Year. Dublin notes the influence technology has had on Carnival. She sees Carnival as an art that brings together different communities to share the beauty of the Caribbean culture. Interview conducted by Michael Roberts.

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Terry Evelyn, born in 1936, was the designer for the Brooklyn Carnival mas band, Hawks International. A native of Trinidad, he has been in the United States since 1964. Recognized as a prodigy in art and mathematics, he began his architectural/design career by designing steel pans. As a child, he saw Carnival in Trinidad as an opportunity to practice and display his artistic skills. He spent his career as an architect and carnival designer. Evelyn's first job in the States was with Standard Oil. As late as 2010, he remained a vocal proponent of Carnival as a meaningful cultural event for Brooklyn.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: In the interview, Terry Evelyn speaks strongly about culture, Carnival, race, and ethnicity. He begins by reflecting on his own origins and his early participation in Trinidad's Carnival. Evelyn compares his experience with the judging process for that event with the process in Brooklyn's Carnival. He discusses mounting a presentation for Nelson Mandela's visit to the United Nations that couldn't be executed. He recalls his early participation and the stakeholders involved with Brooklyn's early Carnivals. In 1994, Evelyn was in high demand for his designs and consulting work in several North American Carnivals, and he relates details about that. He bemoans that Carnival could be turned into a parade of nudity. Evelyn discusses his architectural design for a proposed performance space in Trinidad. He also expresses intolerance towards Jewish residents of Brooklyn and theorizes about conspiracies relating to Jewish influence, war, liberty, and the oppression of African Americans and Caribbean Americans. Interview conducted by Dwan Reece King.

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Elimus "Inspector" Gilbert was born in the parish of St. Patrick in Grenada. In 1985, at age fifteen, Gilbert won the Junior Calypso Monarch and Road March King titles during Carnival in Grenada. He went on to win many more titles, including the Calypso King of Grenada. He is a well-known Grenadian musician and received a Lifetime Achievement Award at the 2026 Grenada Music Awards. As of 2026, Gilbert continues to record and perform Calypso.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: In the interview, Elimus Gilbert thinks that spectator interest in the Labor Day Carnival parade in Brooklyn is dwindling because of the potential for violence. He believes the West Indian American Day Carnival Association has done a decent job, but there are areas that need improvement. Gilbert would like spectators to refrain from joining mas bands before they reach the reviewing stands.

Gilbert supports non-West Indian people getting involved in the Carnival. He observes that the event has been underrepresented in the mainstream media and he wants that changed. Interview conducted by Michael Roberts.

dao.xlink:title: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Carlos Lezama

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Carlos Lezama

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Carlos Lezama was born in 1923 in Coro, Venezuela. He grew up in Trinidad but later returned to Venezuela, where he was an auto worker for General Motors and Chrysler, as well as a mechanic in Caracas specializing in dental machinery. After that, he departed for a job as a merchant mariner. It was during his travels as a seaman that he first visited the United States and eventually resolved to move to New York City, which he did, alone, in 1954. He had lived in Manhattan for about two years when he moved to Crown Heights after noticing the greater movement of Caribbean people into the neighborhood. Soon after his move, his wife and children joined him. They were all congregants at Saint Gregory Catholic Church. He continued to work as a mechanic, taking vocational courses to supplement his training, and bought a home on St. Johns Place. During this time, he became a prominent figure in the cultural life of the West Indian residents of Crown Heights.

Along with Rufus (Lionel) Gorin, he was a key organizer of the first Carnival parade on Eastern Parkway, now commonly known as the West Indian American Day Parade, in 1969. When Gorin died, Lezama was elected the first president of the West Indian American Day Carnival Association (WIADCA), a position he held until his retirement in 2002. He died in 2007.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Lezama, who in 1994 was in his twenty-eighth year as president of the West Indian-American Day Carnival Association (WIADCA), recounts the Carnival's history and his personal involvement. He explains the relocation of the Carnival from Harlem to the Brooklyn neighborhood of Crown Heights and its transformation from a small affair, held mostly indoors in the middle of winter, to a late-summer street festival attracting millions of spectators and participants. He compares the Brooklyn Carnival with its analogs throughout the Caribbean and the United States, especially Trinidad. He describes WIADCA's relationship with city government and the police, both in the aftermath of the 1991 Crown Heights unrest and more recently amid an NYPD "crackdown" on "quality of life" offenses that have affected Carnival participation. He dwells on a dispute with the Hasidim of Crown Heights over the date of the 1994 Carnival, which the Chabad Lubavitch community claimed would conflict with the holiday of Rosh Hashanah, and how newspapers have commented on it. Interview conducted by Dwan Reece King.

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Wesley Millington was born in St. Vincent in 1954. He moved to Brooklyn in 1969 and is a founding member and designer for Mas Productions Unlimited, which in 1994 was a smaller band with a membership of about fifteen.

As of 2026, Millington continues to lead and design for Mas Production Unlimited. The band focuses on child masqueraders and creates costumes for the Kiddies Carnival. Mas Productions Unlimited operates out of a mas camp in Canarsie, Brooklyn.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: In the interview, Wesley Millington discusses his design experience and his desire to bring more creativity to Carnival in Brooklyn. He describes the group's inner workings, noting that one goal is to involve more women in the organization. Millington also mentions the difficulty of getting other Vincentians interested and involved in his organizations. Millington feels that the West Indian American Day Carnival Association could do more to promote and encourage people from other islands to participate in Carnival. daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Kelvin Pope

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Kelvin Pope, also known as "The Mighty Duke," was born in Port Fortin, Trinidad, to parents from St. Vincent. Pope was an internationally acclaimed calypso singer who won four consecutive Calypso Monarch awards in Trinidad. He participated in carnivals around the world, including the West Indian American Day Carnival in Brooklyn, New York. He began participating in the Brooklyn Carnival in 1969. Kelvin Pope died in 2009.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: In this interview, Kelvin Pope discusses his calypso career, from its early start in the Calypso Monarch competitions in Trinidad to his projects as of 1995, the year of this interview. He reminisces about his participation in Carnival, as a mas player and as a musician. He comments on the evolution of calypso in the years leading up to the interview and the emergence of technological advancements in mas costumes and music. Pope discusses the early years of the West Indian American Day Carnival in Brooklyn and compares the contemporary Carnival to Carnival in Trinidad, Notting Hill and Toronto. He notes possible ways to make the Brooklyn Carnival more accessible. Pope also suggests the need for education in handling the continuing conflict that the West Indian American Day Carnival Association has had with its Hasidic Jewish neighbors. Pope also suggests ways the association could partner with city government to ease the Carnival's financial and structural burdens. Interview conducted by Michael Roberts.

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Joyce Quamina was born in Port of Spain, Trinidad. In 1969, she immigrated to the United States and settled in Brooklyn, New York. A Carnival participant in her native Trinidad, Quamina first watched the original West Indian American parades in Harlem, New York, and became an active participant when the parade began in Brooklyn, New York. In 1994, at the time of the interview, she was the business manager of the West Indian American Day Carnival Association (WIADCA). Quamina was the founder and organizer of the Carnival's Kiddies Carnival, an event in which children between the ages of infancy and sixteen participate in their own mas. She also contributed to the Westchester County Caribbean Carnival in White Plains, New York. After retiring from WIADCA, Quamina continued as a business consultant for the association. She passed away in 2022.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Joyce Quamina completed two interviews. In her first interview, Quamina discusses her childhood and adult experiences of Carnival in Trinidad. She relates memories of the West Indian Carnival in Harlem and provides a history of the Brooklyn West Indian American Day Carnival and its Kiddies Carnival, which she founded. She explains why the West Indian American Day Carnival is important to her. She also discusses what she views as key factors in the Carnival's success. Quamina discusses the Carnival's cultural diversity. Given the Carnival's popularity and the revenue it generates for the Crown Heights community and the City of New York, she sees a need for stronger sponsorship and media recognition beyond Brooklyn. The interview ends in a discussion of her role as business manager at the West Indian American Day Carnival Association. Interview conducted by Bill Pincheon.

In her second interview, Quamina provides a more in depth discussion of her role as the West Indian American Day Carnival Association business manager. She discusses the process of registering vendors, gathering information for the press and media outlets, and booking performers for concerts held behind the Brooklyn Museum. Quamina relates her experiences launching the Kiddies Carnival and the Junior Steel Band Panorama, noting the importance of each in sustaining the Carnival and providing summer activities for community children. She assesses the Carnival's future challenges, noting that securing consistent sponsorship will remain central to its survival. Quamina discusses the history of the pan steel band in Trinidad and the United States, specifically addressing the role of girls and women. She also shares her views on the ongoing cultural conflict between the Hasidic Jewish and West Indian communities of Crown Heights. Interview conducted by Bill Pincheon.

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Michelle Quamina Reid

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Michelle Quamina Reid was born in Trinidad. In 1970, she immigrated to Brooklyn, New York, with her mother, Joyce Quamina. Reid had participated in the Carnival in Trinidad and, at the time of this interview in 1994, was an active participant of the West Indian American Day Carnival parade in Brooklyn. Her involvement included active membership in the West Indian American Day Carnival Association, where her mother Joyce was the business manager.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: In this interview, Michelle Quamina Reid reminisces about participating in Carnival as a child in Trinidad and her experience of the West Indian American Carnival in Harlem, New York. She discusses the origins of the West Indian American Day Carnival in Brooklyn, how her mother, Joyce Quamina, became involved in the West Indian American Day Carnival Association (WIADCA), and her own playing of mas. Reid judged the Saturday event, the West Indian American Day Kiddies Carnival. She assisted her mother, Joyce Quamina, in registering vendors for Labor Day and in Be Aware of School, a program founded by Quamina to raise awareness of the importance of school and staying away from drugs. She provides an in-depth description of how the costumed Carnival mas bands were judged. Reid offers opinions on the importance of Carnival to Caribbean heritage, the conflict that arose in 1994 with the religious Jewish community of Crown Heights, and how the different viewpoints of the next generation of WIADCA volunteers may affect the future of Carnival. Interview conducted by Dwan Reece King.

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Kwame Remy

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Kwame Remy was born in Brooklyn, New York. Raised in the Crown Heights neighborhood of Brooklyn, he participated in the West Indian American Day Carnival festivities from the age of three, beginning with the Kiddie Carnival. In 1994, at the time of the interview, he was an eighteen-year-old senior at Sheepshead Bay High School. Remy was deeply involved in the mas competitions, winning prizes for elaborate costumes designed by Trinidadian designer Follette Eustace. He also worked for Joyce Quamina, the business manager for the West Indian American Day Carnival Association (WIADCA) in their administrative offices. Remy was involved in theater, music, and dance. As of 2026, Kwame is a vocalist, actor, and recording artist.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: In this interview, Kwame Remy discusses his involvement in mas performance at Brooklyn's West Indian American Day Carnival. He explains the process of choosing a costume and theme for the mas and, in particular, his experiences with Follette Eustace, an acclaimed Trinidadian designer. Remy expresses frustrations with working in the office of the West Indian American Day Carnival Association and with the general organization of the Carnival. He also notes the conflicts between the cultural communities of Crown Heights. Kwame reflects on the changes he has seen in his fifteen years of participation and on changes he would like to see, including more local and citywide recognition. He also discusses the emergence of DJ music on the floats, the need for bands to respect the time restraints of the Carnival permits, and the rising interracial participation at the event. Interview conducted by Dwan Reece King.

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Yvette Rennie

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Yvette Rennie was born in Trinidad and Tobago. In 1969, she immigrated to the United States to attend Howard University in Washington, D.C. In 1970, she traveled to New York, where she settled in Brooklyn and attended New York Community College before transferring to Brooklyn College. Rennie became involved in political activism surrounding her Caribbean and Black identity and joined Hawks International, a community organization and mas band in Brooklyn. Rennie is also President of J'ouvert City International and helped launch Brooklyn J'Ouvert, an early-morning celebration that signals the start of carnival.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: In this interview, Yvette Rennie discusses her immigration to the United States, the struggles of gaining a footing as an immigrant, and her early participation in the West Indian American Day Carnival. She defines the purpose of the Carnival and suggests that broader knowledge of its history would ease the community tensions the Carnival creates, including the lack of respect and recognition she feels it receives. She also explains Jab Jab, a masquerade form, and J'ouvert, the predawn precursor to the Carnival parade. Rennie notes the contributions of the Carnival participants to the character and economy of the city. She reflects on the police presence at the 1994 Carnival and the possibility of the New York City government subsidizing the event and becoming more involved in organizing the Carnival. The interview concludes with a discussion of what would improve the Carnival. Interview conducted by Michael Roberts.

dao.xlink:title: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Michael Roberts

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Michael Roberts

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Michael Roberts was born in St. George, Grenada. He immigrated to the United States in 1988 and settled in Brooklyn. A journalist for most of his adult life, he served as managing editor of New York Carib News and is currently the Associate Editor of the Caribbean Times. Roberts is also a member of the West Indian American Day Carnival Association and worked closely with Carlos Lezama to help plan Brooklyn's Carnival.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: In this interview, Michael Roberts describes his involvement in the West Indian American Day Carnival in Brooklyn as a member of the press and the West Indian American Day Carnival Association (WIADCA). He addresses the lack of media attention the Carnival receives and notes the unrecognized political and economic power the Carnival signifies for the Caribbean community. Roberts also offers his views on the cultural conflicts between the Caribbean and Hasidic communities in the Crown Heights neighborhood of Brooklyn, which hosts Carnival. Roberts describes Carnival in Grenada, providing a history of its various facets, and compares it to the Brooklyn manifestation. He reflects on the validation of Caribbean cultural identity that Carnival provides and notes its unifying qualities for the Caribbean and African American communities. He also discusses the racial disparity that hinders the Brooklyn Carnival from becoming as racially diverse as Caribbean Carnivals. The interview ends in a discussion of the need for a new generation of leadership for WIADCA and speculation on possible future changes to the parade. Interview conducted by Dwan Reece King.

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: An Italian American, Frank Seddio was born in Brooklyn's Canarsie neighborhood. A lifelong New York City civil servant, he served as a police officer, community board chairman, State Assemblyman, district court judge, and Chairman of the Kings County Democratic Party. Seddio was instrumental in the early phases of Brooklyn'sWest Indian American Day Carnival. From 1969-1970, as the community involvement liaison for the New York Police Department, he worked with Carlos Lezama to organize the Carnival's logistics. He later became a consultant for the West Indian American Day Carnival Association (WIADCA). When interviewed in 1994, Seddio was the Chairman of Community Board 18 in Brooklyn and legal counsel for the WIADCA.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: In this interview, Frank Seddio reflects on his early experiences and contributions to Brooklyn's Carnival. A former police officer who handled the Carnival's civil logistics, he describes the early challenges of running it, including political and police department resistance to recognizing the Carnival as a community festival. He reflects on the need to constantly reassess and reformulate the event in its early phases, and how it has continued to change over his twenty-five years of involvement. He also describes the policies and training the Carnival's context required of New York police officers. The interview ends with a reflection on how his involvement in the Carnival has given him unique insight into the Caribbean community. He notes that the larger New York City community must recognize the Caribbean community's and the Carnival's contribution to the fabric of New York. Interview conducted by Maureen Mahon.

dao.xlink:title: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Charles Simpson

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Charles Simpson

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Charles Simpson was born in Kingston, Jamaica. He has been a regular visitor to Trinidad and Tobago over the years, where he has been actively involved in Carnival. Simpson was a founder of the West Indies International Association and, previously a soldier in the Jamaica Defense Force, the ex-West Indian Servicemen Association. Simpson is one of the pioneers of Jamaica Carnival, which formed in 1990.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Charles Simpson says in his interview that the West Indian American Day Carnival Association is doing a great job, as shown by the tremendous numbers who flock to Eastern Parkway every year at Labor Day to witness and participate in Brooklyn's Carnival. He sees organizational problems, but acknowledges that, given the size of the event, this is inevitable. Simpson recalls his involvement in this Carnival over the years at various levels, and he says this collective experience helped him become a key player in building the Jamaica Carnival, which takes place in April. He feels city government can do more, and he also thinks the Carnival deserves better press, TV coverage, and input from the business sector through sponsorship. He argues that big business gets involved with the Macy's Parade and similar events, which, in his view, cannot compare with the Labor Day Carnival Parade at any level. Interview conducted by Michael Roberts.

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Frank Smith

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Frank Smith was born in Trinidad and Tobago. He immigrated to the United States in his thirties to care for his father, who was residing in Brooklyn. Smith participated in the West Indian American Day Carnival as an organizer and promoter of tents and Calypso performances. At the time of this interview in 1994, Smith had recently closed his nightclub, the Rainbow Terrace (1978-1993), which was a famous venue that showcased calypso and American performers. Smith also owned a gas station, CLR Auto Service, on Fulton Street in Brooklyn. He passed away in 2015.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: In this interview, Frank Smith recalls immigrating to the United States, his first impressions of Brooklyn, and his work promoting calypso music for the West Indian American Day Carnival. Smith discusses changes he has seen in the Carnival, his attempts to coordinate a mas band, and his efforts to recruit talent for his calypso nightclub and the Carnival. He compares the Toronto Carnival, Caribana, to the Brooklyn Carnival, noting the differences and suggesting ways Brooklyn could better its participant route. Smith also discusses using masks and costumes from the Labor Day event to participate in the Fulton Street Festival. This event occurred approximately two weeks after the West Indian American Day Carnival. Interview conducted by Dwan Reece King.

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Dr. Lamuel Stanislaus was born in Grenada in 1921. He immigrated to the United States in 1945 to attend Howard University, where he earned a degree in dentistry. After receiving his degree, he moved to Brooklyn, where he maintained a dental practice for forty-three years. A founding member of the West Indian American Day Carnival Association, Dr. Stanislaus was also the United Nations Ambassador to Grenada from 1985 to 1990. At the time of this 1994 interview, he had recently retired from practice. Dr. Stanislaus died in 2016.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: In this interview, Dr. Lamuel Stanislaus describes his personal life and relates the history of the Carnival in its European and African roots. He describes his first impression of the West Indian American Day festivities in Harlem, New York, in the 1940s, and the events that led to the creation of the West Indian American Day Carnival and its parent association in Brooklyn. Dr. Stanislaus discusses the Carnival's planning process. He explains that, in 1994, the Carnival coincided with the Jewish holiday of Rosh Hashanah. This created a conflict between Carnival organizers and members of the Hasidic Jewish community of Crown Heights in Brooklyn. Dr. Stanislaus offers his perspective on this situation and on the Crown Heights riot of 1991. He speculates on the Carnival's potential political influence and discusses how the event can support charities in the community and around the world. Interview conducted by Dwan Reece King.

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Tricia Thomas

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Tricia Thomas was born in New York City. From age two to six, she lived in Trinidad. Her family then returned to New York to live in Brooklyn. At the time of the interview, she was sixteen years old and living in Edison, New Jersey. Many of her family members participated in Brooklyn's Carnival as masqueraders with Hawks International. Thomas was a member of the steel pan youth band, Caribbean American Sports and Cultural Youth Movement (CASYM), which required her to make multiple weekly visits to Brooklyn for rehearsals and to commit to prolonged stays during the summer season before Carnival.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: In this interview, Tricia Thomas discusses her participation in Brooklyn's Carnival and in playing mas, the themed costume participation, from the age of three. She reflects on her choice to play the steel pan rather than mas and describes her family's participation in Carnival. A participant or observer of Carnival in a number of cities, she provides her opinion on the differences in the Carnivals and notes the pros and cons of each. Noting the lack of media recognition of the Carnival, Thomas sees a need for the New York population to acknowledge and respect the Caribbean community's desire to preserve the cultural meaning of Carnival. Interview conducted by Dwan Reece King.

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Jay Thompson was born in St. Kitts. She moved to New York as a teenager and lived there from age fourteen to seventeen before returning to St. Kitts. After finishing school and working for the government of St. Kitts, Thompson returned to New York City at the age of twenty-three. Thompson does not play mas in Brooklyn's Carnival, but attends as a booth operator selling West Indian food. In 1994, when the interview took place, Thompson lived in the Bronx with her two children.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents

She notes that her booth is a central meeting place for St. Kittitians. Thompson also says the booth did not operate during the 1994 Carnival because of cost and time constraints imposed that year, stemming from a conflict with the Jewish community's celebration of Rosh Hashanah. She also discusses the St. Kitts Carnival, which occurs between Christmas and New Year's. Interview conducted by Maureen Mahon.

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Joyce Toney

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Joyce Toney was born in St. Vincent & the Grenadines. She immigrated to the United States to attend college in the Midwest and moved to Brooklyn in 1972, where she began teaching high school, working for nonprofit organizations, and attending graduate school. At the time of this interview in 1994, Joyce Toney was a professor in the Department of Africana & Puerto Rican/Latino Studies at the City University of New York, Hunter College. Professor Toney served as chairperson of that department from 1998-2002 and as director of the Women Studies program at the same college from 2002-2005.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: In this interview, Joyce Toney discusses her participation in the carnivals in Brooklyn, Toronto, and St. Vincent, noting the differences between the events. She also considers how the structure of the carnivals in Toronto and St. Vincent could alleviate the difficulties of the West Indian American Day Carnival in Brooklyn, New York. Toney reminisces about starting a "band," a musical group of mas players (the costumed participants of Carnival), in the 1970s. She discusses the definition of carnival, describing the process of playing mas. Toney discusses the camaraderie between mas players, noting that togetherness in mas does not necessarily signify a unified Caribbean community. She discusses the politicization of Carnival and the potential to use Carnival's popularity to advance the needs of the Caribbean community. The interview ends in a discussion of Carnival as an expression of Caribbean identity. Interview conducted by Maureen Mahon.

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Daphne Weeks was born in Port of Spain, Trinidad, and immigrated to the United States in 1947. Weeks was a well-known pianist in Trinidad and became a calypso bandleader in the U.S. Her band, Daphne Weeks and Her Versatile Caribbean Band, performed in the Harlem West Indian American parade and masquerade balls. She also participated in the Brooklyn West Indian American Day Carnival for twenty-six years and served as a featured judge in the Carnival's steel band competition. Daphne Weeks died on October 8, 2004.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: In this interview, Daphne Weeks describes her musical career in Trinidad and her immigration to the United States. After settling in Brooklyn, she played jazz and calypso in Harlem's big-band clubs. Early in her career, Weeks met Count Basie, Duke Ellington, and Billie Holiday. She also reflects on many West Indian American musicians of the period, such as Don Wilson, Lankey Belasco, Ohaldo Williams, and Willie Gayle. Weeks discusses her participation in the earlier West Indian parade in Harlem, relating her experiences with the founder Jessie Wattle and Wattle's successor Evans Butcher. She describes the event that may have ended the parades in Harlem and recalls the meeting between Rufus Gorin and Carlos Lezama that launched the Brooklyn Carnival. She also defines and discusses the Dame Lorraine dances that once concluded the Carnival parades. Weeks discusses her twenty-six-year participation in the Brooklyn West Indian American Day Carnival, noting the changes in the parade. She reflects on the police's relationship to the Carnival community and offers her view of what causes conflict between parade spectators and the police. The interview ends with Daphne Weeks returning to a discussion of her musical career. Interview conducted by Bill Pincheon.

dao.xlink:title: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Gailene Windsor

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Gailene Windsor

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Gailene Windsor was born in St. Vincent & the Grenadines. She moved to Brooklyn, New York, in 1979. At the time of her 1995 interview, Windsor was very active in the Vincentian community abroad, acting as the general secretary of a Vincentian-based New York Carnival organization. She played mas in St. Vincent and in the West Indian American Day Carnival in Brooklyn. In 2016, Windsor joined the non-governmental organization The St. Vincent & Grenadines Diaspora Committee of New York.

Windsor was also a professional netballer in St. Vincent & the Grenadines and held posts such as the president of the American Netball Association, co-founder of the Caribbean American Netball Association, president of the United States International Netball, and secretary of the Brooklyn Soccer League and Caribbean Cup. Windsor returned to St. Vincent & the Grenadines in 2018, and passed away in 2020.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The interview begins with Gailene Windsor considering the political reasons the Carnival in St. Vincent has declined in the years before 1995 and how the island's economy will be affected by the lack of Vincentian diaspora in the event. She discusses her involvement in promoting Vincentian culture and her participation in the Brooklyn West Indian American Day Carnival. Windsor notes the lack of media coverage the Carnival receives and suggests political and community solutions. She addresses cultural conflicts between the Hasidic Jewish and West Indian communities of Crown Heights, suggesting solutions to ease tensions. She also discusses the need for planning and financial support from the local government for the parade, noting that the Caribbean community must unify to gain political power. Windsor addresses technological advancements in Carnival mas costumes and music, noting the loss of steel pan music to soca, calypso, and reggae. Interview conducted by Michael Roberts.
